title: Biophilic design and office planting: a case study of effects on perceived health, well-being and performance metrics in the workplace
research_question: 1. To investigate the impact of plant introduction in offices vs break-out spaces on perceived health, well-being and performance metrics such as attention, creativity, productivity, efficiency, motivation, stress and tiredness. 2. To investigate the impact of plants' removal on perceived health, well-being and performance metrics. 3. To understand occupants' preferences for visual and physical access to plants and satisfaction with overall office design.

participants.description: 27 males and 13 females, aged 21-60 years (mean 31-40 years), spending 1-10 hours (mean 7-10 hours) in their offices, and having occupied the building for 1-6 months. Located in Reading, UK.
participants.recruitment: Participants registered interest within a 4-week inquiry period before the start of the experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Modern office building (3,844 m², four storey, BREEAM 'Outstanding') with individual offices and break-out spaces. Conditions included: 1) Control (no plants), 2) Living plants in individual offices (2 potted plants per person: one small Sedum on desk, one larger species elsewhere) and break-out spaces (8 plants), 3) Living plants only in break-out spaces (8 plants). Plant species included Spathiphyllum wallisii cv. 'Verdi', Dracaena fragrans cv. 'Lemon Lime' and 'Golden Coast', Ficus benjamina, Zamioculcas zamiifolia, Guzmania, and Sedum sp. mix.

findings.antecedent: Introduction/removal of living plants from offices and/or break-out spaces
findings.mechanism: Occupants may have failed to recognize the few potted plants within their field of vision due to habituation or adaptation. These metrics may also not be easily detected using self-report questionnaires.
findings.quote: Our results, however, showed that the introduction into and removal of living plants from offices and/or break-out spaces did not elicit any changes in participants' perceived tiredness, health, well-being or motivation.

mechanisms: Attention Restoration Theory (ART): Mental fatigue from directed attention can be restored by engaging with nature, which uses less energy-intensive involuntary attention.
Stress Recovery Theory (SRT): Views of nature induce more restful brain activity, reducing stress levels and encouraging positive emotional states.
Biophilia hypothesis: Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature, and this connection is vital for health, well-being, and performance.
Improved Indoor Air Quality (IAQ): Living plants can improve air quality, simulating healthy outdoor environments and positively influencing perceived IAQ and health.
Perceived managerial care: The introduction of biophilic elements signals that management is taking an interest in employees' health, well-being, and performance (Hawthorne effect).
moderators: Location of planting (individual offices vs. break-out spaces)
Interactions with plants during break times
implementation_implications: Biophilic design, specifically installing living plants, is a sound financial investment due to potential performance enhancements.
For maximum effect on health, well-being, and performance, a full landscaping approach that does not hamper functionality should be taken to provide constant opportunities for restoration.
Physical and visual access to plants within individual offices and break-out spaces is crucial for occupant satisfaction.
Plant placement should avoid obstructing functional use of space (e.g., coffee tables) to maximize restorative effects.

limitations: The study relied solely on qualitative subjective measures (self-report questionnaires) rather than objective cognitive performance tests or physiological measures.
The study did not investigate the impact of other factors such as positioning, types, sizes, and volumes of plants.
Habituation or adaptation to the presence of plants over time might have occurred, potentially masking effects on perceived health, tiredness, well-being, and motivation.
The placement of plants on coffee tables in break-out spaces might have negated their potential restorative effects by obstructing the tables' use for food or drink.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural elements in the workplace can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue.
Exposure to natural elements in the workplace can reduce physiological and psychological stress.
Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which can lead to positive psychological and physiological outcomes.
